intro.html: Every story has a high point and an ending. These words name the top (zenith, apex, pinnacle), the bottom (nadir) and the moment a long effort reaches its peak (culminate). The rest describe the ways things end: they stop, they die out, or they simply fall out of use.

The top: zenith, apex, pinnacle. The bottom: nadir. Building to the peak: culminate. Ending: terminate, cessation, demise. Out of use: obsolete (out of date) and defunct (no longer existing or working).

words.def: to reach the highest point or the final, biggest stage
words.ex: A week of rehearsals {culminated} in a standing ovation on opening night.
words.ctx: The long effort to save the old theater {culminated} in a grand reopening, with the whole town packed inside for the first show in twenty years.
words.etym: From Late Latin culminare, “to crown, to reach the top,” from Latin culmen, “top, summit.”

mn.cue: CLIMB-inate: it CLIMBS to the big finish
mn.text: The fireworks show climbs higher and higher and ends with one giant golden burst: the show {culminates} in a grand finale.

scene.alt: Two children cheer as a fireworks show ends in a giant burst in the night sky.

words.def: to bring to an end, or to come to an end
words.ex: The bus line {terminates} at the edge of town, so we walked the last mile.
words.ctx: After the third broken promise, the bakery decided to {terminate} its deal with the flour supplier and find a more reliable one.
words.etym: From Latin terminare, “to set a limit, to end,” from terminus, “boundary, end.”

mn.cue: TERMIN-al: the END of the line
mn.text: The train pulls into the terminal, the very end of the line. “Everybody off!” The trip {terminates} here.

scene.alt: A train conductor waves at the last stop while a grandmother steps off with her suitcase.

words.def: a stopping; the end of something
words.ex: The {cessation} of the rain brought everyone out onto their porches.
words.ctx: After months of construction next door, the sudden {cessation} of the hammering felt strange; the street was so quiet that the birds could be heard again.

roots.means: stop (from Latin cedere, to go, to yield)

words.etym: From Latin cessatio, “a stopping,” from cessare, “to stop, to hold back,” the source of cease.

mn.text: The rain ceases, a rainbow appears, and Nell shakes out her umbrella. The {cessation} of the storm brings everyone outside.

scene.alt: When the rain stops, a woman lifts her umbrella and a toddler jumps in a puddle under a rainbow.

words.def: the end of something; also, a death
words.ex: The arrival of the big new mall led to the {demise} of the little corner bookshop.
words.ctx: Once every family carried a phone in a pocket, the {demise} of the phone booth was only a matter of time; by the end, hardly anyone could find one.
words.etym: From Anglo-French demis, “sent away, handed over,” from Latin dimittere, “to send away.”

mn.cue: DE-MIZE: his SIZE goes DOWN to nothing
mn.text: In the spring sun, the snowman’s size shrinks down, down, down, until only a puddle, a hat and a carrot are left. That is the snowman’s {demise}.

scene.alt: A girl kneels sadly beside a snowman that is melting into a puddle in the spring sun.

words.def: no longer used or useful; out of date
words.ex: Grandpa still keeps his {obsolete} typewriter on a shelf in the den.
words.ctx: The old road map was {obsolete}; three highways had been built since it was printed, and the bridge it showed had been torn down years ago.
words.etym: From Latin obsoletus, “worn out, grown old.”

mn.text: At the museum, Dev stares at a giant old radio the size of a fridge. Nobody uses one like that anymore: it is {obsolete}.

scene.alt: A teen with a phone stares, puzzled, at a huge old radio on display in a museum.

words.def: no longer existing, working or in use
words.ex: The {defunct} factory has been turned into apartments and a bakery.
words.ctx: Weeds grew between the rails of the {defunct} railway line; no train had run there in thirty years, and the station clock had stopped at a quarter past four.
words.etym: From Latin defunctus, “finished, dead,” from defungi, “to finish one’s work”: de (off) + fungi (to perform).

mn.text: The old robot in the alley no longer functions: no lights, no beeps, just a puff of dust. It is {defunct}.

scene.alt: A woman points at a broken old robot leaning in an alley, a puff of smoke rising from its head.

words.def: the highest point; the time of greatest success or power
words.ex: At its {zenith}, the little bakery sold a thousand loaves a day.
words.ctx: The singer’s career reached its {zenith} in her forties, when every concert sold out within minutes; after that, she chose to sing only for small crowds.
words.etym: From an Arabic phrase meaning “the path over the head,” which reached English through Old Spanish and Medieval Latin.
words.note: In astronomy, the zenith is the point in the sky straight overhead; the nadir is the point straight below.

mn.text: From the very top of the peak, with the sun straight overhead, Maya can see everything beneath her. She has reached the {zenith}.

scene.alt: A hiker cheers on the very top of a mountain peak with the sun straight overhead.

words.def: the top or highest point, often a pointed tip
words.ex: The lion is called an {apex} predator because no other animal hunts it.
words.ctx: The pyramid narrowed as it rose, and at its {apex}, the very tip, the builders set a single gleaming capstone.

mn.cue: APE-X: the APE on the very tip
mn.text: A cheeky ape scrambles up to the pointed tip of the pyramid and waves: he has reached the {apex}.

labels.text: APE-X: the APE at the TIP

scene.alt: A monkey stands on the pointed tip of a pyramid in the desert.

words.def: the highest point of success or achievement
words.ex: Winning the state title was the {pinnacle} of Coach Omar’s career.
words.ctx: For a young violinist, a solo with the city orchestra is the {pinnacle}; there is no higher honor in the whole state.
words.etym: From Late Latin pinnaculum, a little peak or gable on a building.

mn.cue: a PIN and a CUP: the very top
mn.text: Rosa wins the gold pin and the giant cup at the national meet, the highest honor of all: the {pinnacle} of her career.

scene.alt: A champion with a gold medal holds up a trophy on the winner's stand while her friends clap.

words.ex: The team’s {nadir} came in October, when it lost five games in a row.
words.ctx: After the flood, the town was at its {nadir}: shops were boarded up, roads were washed out and many families had moved away; yet within five years it had bounced back.
words.etym: From an Arabic phrase meaning “opposite the zenith.”
words.note: Nadir and zenith are opposites: the lowest point and the highest.

mn.text: Kai has spent every last coin. He shakes his piggy bank and gets nada, nothing at all: his savings have hit their {nadir}.

scene.alt: A sad boy sits on the floor shaking an empty piggy bank.

what it names

after.html: Zenith and nadir are opposites: the highest point and the lowest. Culminate does not simply mean to end; it means to reach the high point that a long effort has been building toward (the season culminated in a championship). And obsolete things still exist but are out of date, while defunct things no longer exist or work at all.

opts.s: Years of practice {culminated} in a gold medal at the national championship.
opts.why: The practice built up to its high point, the gold medal: it culminated.

items.q: Losing ten games in a row was the ______ of the team’s season. Which word fits?
items.why: A losing streak is a low point: the nadir. Zenith, apex and pinnacle all name high points.

items.q: True or false: culminate simply means to stop.
items.why: False. To culminate is to reach the highest point or final stage, the big finish that an effort builds toward.

items.q: The toy company closed its doors for good in 1990. The company is…
items.why: A business that no longer exists is defunct. Obsolete describes things that still exist but are out of date, like a typewriter.

items.q: Cessation is the noun that goes with which verb?
items.why: A cessation is a ceasing: a stop. Both come from Latin cessare, to stop.

items.q: Type the word for the lowest point, the opposite of zenith.
items.why: The nadir is the lowest point; the zenith is the highest.
